claim: Of 94,371 Steam releases 2016-2025 most titles are 1-3 words; title length does not correlate with sales; ~13% use a colon subtitle. Steam and Google find games by exact name, so SEO matters less than festivals/streamers/social. Advice: short, easy to say and spell, test by saying it aloud and having someone write it down; avoid invented spellings, emoji and generic-word chains; name unique enough to search.
example: Skyrim Special Edition (43 chars) sells fine; six one-character titles exist and get no sales benefit

claim: Vendor-blog guidance (commercial interest): check the candidate on Steam, app stores, domains, social handles and trademark before committing; players should be able to pronounce, spell, search and repeat it. Renaming a Steam page later is possible, a released demo is harder.
Developer forum advice: google the candidate and see what already comes up before committing.
PC Gamer headline piece on Steam games with weirdly similar, forgettable names; body not retrievable (fetch returned only site chrome), so no claim from its content beyond the topic.

A study of ~20,000 AI-generated stories found the same ~11 words (names such as Elias, Mara, Elara; occupations such as lighthouse keeper, clockmaker, librarian) in over 88% of stories with little difference between models: evidence that model output converges on a small stock vocabulary. About names and story nouns, not game titles; no measured study of LLM game titles found.

No official account of the title found. Critic reads it as the -punk suffix convention (cyberpunk, steampunk) applied to the setting (frost); working title during development was 'Industrial'. Shows a title can be a genre-label template plus a setting word, the pattern the reviewer calls trend-suffix.
Title and concept both draw from Bostrom's 2003 paperclip maximizer thought experiment: the name is the mechanic's own idea. Creator's own statement on choosing the title not found.
example: Universal Paperclips: from the paperclip maximizer thought experiment

claim: Title is the in-fiction place the plot is about: a mysterious road (Route Zero) the protagonist must find. Combines a real-sounding place format (state + route number) with a fictional twist. No developer account of naming found.
example: Kentucky Route Zero: a fictional road in the game

claim: Original title was No Truce With The Furies, renamed in 2018; reason not found in results. Shows even strong titles can be reworked late.
example: Disco Elysium (formerly No Truce With The Furies)

claim: Character came first (a Knight from the jam game Hungry Knight), the game was designed around him, and the title names the story's chosen vessel. No developer statement on the title itself found.
example: Hollow Knight: character from a game-jam prototype, name from in-world lore term

claim: Null: no developer account of why it is called A Dark Room found; the title is the opening situation of the game (you wake in a dark room). That reading is inference, not sourced.
example: A Dark Room: the starting scene

claim: Authors routinely take titles from a phrase in earlier literature (Shakespeare, the Bible, poems), either as allusion to the older work's themes or because the phrase is memorable. Nothing found on game developers doing this or on mining childhood reading specifically.
example: Brave New World from The Tempest; Absalom, Absalom! from 2 Samuel
